OrthoWatch — post-market surveillance of orthopedic device reports

FDA MAUDE, 2020–2024 · control-chart trending · PRR/ROR signals · narrative mining

Published

August 22, 2026

What this is

84,547 cleaned adverse event reports on orthopedic devices, drawn from the FDA’s MAUDE database (2020-01 to 2024-12) and screened three ways: when did reporting move (control charts), what problems attach to which device families (disproportionality statistics), and what the free-text narratives say that the coded fields don’t (text mining).

Read this first. MAUDE reports are unverified reporter submissions. Counts reflect reporting behavior as much as device performance; report volume says nothing about how many devices are in use. Every flag and signal below means investigate — never unsafe — and nothing in this report is a finding about any product.

When: monthly trends against control limits

Each family’s monthly report count, with a band at the mean ± 3 standard deviations — the century-old control-chart convention: ordinary randomness lives inside the band; points outside deserve a question.

Two caveats the numbers themselves taught: these series trend strongly, and a single five-year mean over-flags trending series (152 of 240 months flag — rolling-baseline limits are the documented refinement on the roadmap); and the tallest towers here turned out, on investigation, to reflect reporting behavior — batch submissions concentrated in single reporters — rather than devices deteriorating.

What: disproportionality signals (PRR/ROR)

For every (family, problem) pair, the 2×2-table statistics standard in vigilance, judged by the published Evans rule (PRR ≥ 2, χ² ≥ 4, at least 3 reports). Because each family is its own denominator, these are immune to the volume trends above.

Spinal fixation Device Slipped 571 28.2 30.1 25.4 35.7
Hip prosthesis Biocompatibility 1001 21.9 22.6 18.0 28.4
Hip prosthesis Corroded 908 20.6 21.2 16.8 26.8
Spinal fixation Material Integrity Problem 236 19.2 19.7 15.6 24.8

Bone plate Difficult to Advance 39 14.3 14.4 8.2 25.2

Bone plate Entrapment of Device 100 8.7 8.8 6.5 11.8
Spinal fixation Compatibility Problem 109 8.6 8.7 6.7 11.4

The 64 passing pairs cohere clinically — a metal-degradation cluster for hips, slippage and integrity for spinal fixation, wear and instability for knees, an intraoperative-fit cluster for bone plates — and the method validates itself: the dataset’s largest, vaguest problem category signals for no family, exactly as a category present everywhere should. Over-reported ≠ over-occurring: signals open investigations, never close them.

What the stories say: narrative vocabulary

The coded fields are the tip of each report; the free-text narrative is the substance. After tokenizing the narratives and stripping filler, each family’s most distinctive words (rate in the family vs. everyone else — the same 2×2 arithmetic, applied to vocabulary):

Text mining’s two contributions here: it exposed a subpopulation the codes hid (the bone-plate family contains a large craniofacial/mandibular plating subgroup), and it corroborated the coded signals from an independent direction (hip narratives orbit a metal-on-metal resurfacing device class by name). It also settled two open questions by reading: the vague-coded reports’ stories often contain specifics the codes omit, and one odd spinal signal traced to a single reporter’s legal-disclaimer template — a reporting pattern, not a device pattern.

How this report was made

This is an executable document: rendering it re-runs every query and figure against data/processed/orthowatch.db, which is itself rebuilt by a one-command pipeline (Rscript run_pipeline.R) whose final stage is the project’s 50-test suite. Same raw files in, same report out. Source, tutorials, and the full build story: github.com/akannan2987/orthowatch.
